sources.citation: Blench, Roger M. 2022. The relevance of Bantoid for the reconstruction of Proto-Bantu verbal extensions. In Koen Bostoen, Gilles-Maurice de Schryver, Rozenn Guérois & Sara Pacchiarotti (eds.), On reconstructing Proto-Bantu grammar (Niger-Congo Comparative Studies 4), 235-280. Berlin: Language Science Press. DOI 10.5281/zenodo.7575823 (volume: OAPEN handle 20.500.12657/63273, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.7560553). [= the 'OAPEN Bantoid volume index: Osatu [South-West Grassfields] 261, 272' that A saw in archive.org full text but did not identify or list]
sources.note: Nothing on Osatu prosody or any Osatu form. The only relevant sentence (p.260): 'Momo and South-West within Wider Grassfields remain extremely poorly known and the internal configuration of Grassfields is yet to be demonstrated convincingly.' Verbal-extension data for the South-West group are '? ?' (unknown) with Manta as the sole representative.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. 2016. New research on Tivoid and its place within Bantoid. Slides, Bantu VI, University of Helsinki, 22 June 2016.
sources.note: Nothing. One mention: 'The languages Balo, Manta and Osatu were previously assigned to Tivoid but the evidence for this is unreliable and these are now classified with West Momo, now rebaptised SW Grassfields.' No Osatu data.

sources.note: Nothing. Pop. 400 (2002 SIL); 'Dialects: None known'; lexical similarity 60% Balo, 40% Ipulo/Caka, 35% Mesaka/Esimbi; 'Writing: Unwritten'. No typology field.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger M. 2010. The Momo and 'Western Momo' languages: branches of Grassfields. Draft for comment, Kay Williamson Educational Foundation, Cambridge. 22 pp. (Glottolog ref 33956; the only Glottolog reference for osat1238, Glottolog's most extensive description type 'a wordlist or less')
sources.note: Nothing. Osatu appears in Table 5 (p.11, ISO/names/pop/location), Table 6 (p.12: resource = 'SIL Wordlist'; 'there is no data other than survey data for any of these languages'), Table 7 comparative wordlist column (pp.12-17, untoned) and Fig. 2 classification (p.18). Sec. 1.2 'Phonology' is transcription conventions only; 0 hits for stress/accent.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger (with Mallam Dendo). 2008 [PDF created 2008-04-10; listed in Glottolog as 'Blench, Roger M. 2009. The Tivoid languages: Classification and Comparative Word List. Unpublished ms., 24 pp.' ref 105309]. Tivoid comparative wordlist [first version, including Balo, Batanga, Asaka and Osatu columns; superseded by the Nov 2011/2016 revision that excluded Balo, Manta and Osatu]. Ms., Cambridge: Kay Williamson Educational Foundation. 12 pp. (this layout).
sources.note: No phonology section. p.1: 'Uncorrected forms are not tone-marked.' The Osatu column gives 119 segmental IPA forms (e.g. 1 mouth ɔndo, 2 eye iʃi, 3 head ifi, 7 nose izwi, 43 water ɔmwɔ) with NO tone or stress marks (0 tone diacritics in the Osatu column; Ugare/Esimbi columns are toned). Closing commentary (pp.8-12) concerns Esimbi's membership only. Wordlist-only data; silent on Osatu stress and tone.

sources.citation: Starr, Alan & Clark Regnier. 2008. Tivoid Survey [report on a 1990 SIL survey of Assumbo (Ipulo-Eman-Caka) and Mesaka/Icheve, Akwaya Subdivision]. SIL Electronic Survey Reports 2008-022. Dallas: SIL International. 52 pp. (Glottolog ref 61699, linked there to Ipulo [ass] and Mesaka [iyo] only.)
sources.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
sources.note: No phonology content for Osatu. Osatu occurs only in sec. 1.1 classification ('..along with Tiv (802), Esimbi (803), Manta (804), and Ihatum (Osatu) (899)'), in the Eman multilingualism charts ('Speak Osatu / Comp. Osatu' rows) and p.~20 'the Amanavil people also have a high reported rate of ability in the Caka speech forms and Osatu'. The single 'tone' mention (RTT differences 'in vowel and tone quality') concerns Oliti/Icheve, not Osatu.
